column3: The speaker addresses his heart, and behold also this is futility is a statement without a separate verb proved.
The question is what is this doing rather than explicitly what does it accomplish.
The days of their lives are numbered, without an explicit few; the heart guides in wisdom.
The first object is my works, which he made great.
Close to the Hebrew.
Pools of water are made for himself, to water a forest sprouting trees.
The household-born are called sons of the house.
The final noun occurs in singular and plural forms rather than an explicit phrase many concubines.
Close to the Hebrew.
He withheld nothing from his eyes, rather than changing the object to myself.
Behold introduces the judgment without a separate verb found.
The question names the person who comes after the king, with no explicit more or can do.
Close to the Hebrew.
The single fate happens to all of them, rather than explicitly both.
The question asks why I have become exceedingly wise, rather than explicitly what I have gained.
The wise and fool have no lasting remembrance; the coming days’ forgetting is expressed as already complete.
Close to the Hebrew.
Leaving the toil is expressed with a future verb, without a separate must.
Toiling and acting wisely are separately expressed.
The speaker turns to make his heart despair, rather than the heart alone beginning to despair.
He gives his portion without a separate word must.
The striving is explicitly that of his heart.
His days are pains, and his heart has not lain down at night.
Better than is not separately expressed; enjoying the work is literally showing his soul good in his toil.
The final phrase is apart from me rather than apart from Him.
The giving is expressed as completed.
